Minimizing overlap reduces the complexity of this step [S2, unofficial].

The evidence states that minimizing screen space overlaps is intended to 'reduce subsequent pixel transfer and compositing steps' (Source [S2] passages). The claim, however, asserts that minimizing overlap reduces the 'complexity of this step [S2, unofficial]'. The evidence does not mention 'complexity' in relation to the reduction of overlaps, nor does it define what '[S2, unofficial]' refers to in a way that links it to complexity reduction. Therefore, the specific claim about reducing complexity is not supported by the provided text.
supported
# Predict rendering costs of groups [S2, unofficial]

The claim states that the evidence supports the prediction of rendering costs for groups. The source notes explicitly mention: 'A load balancing technique for sort-first rendering that predicts rendering costs of triangle groups'. Additionally, the passage from Samanta et al. [117] confirms this by stating they 'developed dynamic screen partitioning schemes that predict the rendering costs of groups of triangles'. Since the specific action of predicting rendering costs of groups is directly stated in the evidence, the claim is supported.
supported
# Minimize screen space overlaps to reduce pixel transfer [S2, unofficial]

The claim states that minimizing screen space overlaps reduces pixel transfer. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly supports this in the passage regarding Samanta et al. [116], stating: 'The objectives that they are addressing are balancing the rendering load on the nodes as well as minimizing the screen space overlaps which require the subsequent pixel transfer and compositing step.' This confirms that the overlap leads to pixel transfer, and thus minimizing it reduces that transfer.
supported

Unlike pure sort-first methods that focus on retained-mode databases fitting in graphics hardware memory [S2, unofficial], this approach targets immediate-mode databases larger than host main memory, though the specific implementations discussed still require model replication on rendering nodes [S2, unofficial].

The claim is fully supported by the evidence in Source [S2]. 1. The claim states that pure sort-first methods (like Mueller's) focus on retained-mode databases fitting in graphics hardware memory; the text confirms: 'Mueller... focusing on retained-mode databases that fit in the memory of the graphics hardware.' 2. The claim states this approach targets immediate-mode databases larger than host main memory; the text confirms: 'In contrast, we focus our work on immediate-mode databases that are larger than the main memory of the host hardware.' 3. The claim states that specific implementations discussed still require model replication on rendering nodes; the text confirms regarding Samanta et al.'s earlier work: 'Once again, the geometry is replicated on each of the nodes' and notes the limitation that 'the model had to be replicated in main memory on each of the rendering nodes'.
supported
Mueller focused on retained-mode databases fitting in graphics hardware memory, while Samanta focused on immediate-mode databases larger than main memory [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that Mueller focused on retained-mode databases fitting in graphics hardware memory, while Samanta (referred to as 'the author's work' in the source context) focused on immediate-mode databases larger than main memory. The last paragraph of Source [S2] explicitly states: 'Mueller also worked on the database management problem, focusing on retained-mode databases that fit in the memory of the graphics hardware. In contrast, we focus our work on immediate-mode databases that are larger than the main memory of the host hardware.' Since the source text attributes the 'immediate-mode' focus to the authors of the paper (who are identified earlier in the text as Samanta et al.), the evidence fully supports the claim.
supported
The method operates on a cluster of commodity PCs connected by a high-speed network [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the method operates on a cluster of commodity PCs connected by a high-speed network. Source [S1] explicitly mentions that these systems 'are generally comprised of clusters of inexpensive PCs' and that 'High speed networks were the key to leverage clusters of PCs'. Source [S2] confirms this by stating that Samanta et al. developed a system 'using a network of commodity PCs' and that WireGL sends calls 'over a high-speed network'. Both sources corroborate the hardware (commodity/inexpensive PCs) and connectivity (high-speed network) aspects of the claim.
supported
*   **Limitations:** Geometry replication limits scalability; dynamic partitioning can bottleneck frame rate; model size limited by main memory [S2, unofficial].

The claim consists of three specific limitations: 1) Geometry replication limits scalability, 2) dynamic partitioning can bottleneck frame rate, and 3) model size is limited by main memory. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly supports all three points. First, it states that a limitation of the system was 'the lack of scalability with respect to model size, as the model had to be replicated in main memory on each of the rendering nodes.' Second, it notes that 'the dynamic partitioning phase could become a bottleneck and limit the frame rate.' Third, it confirms that 'neither the preprocessing phase nor the rendering phase would be able to handle a model larger than main memory.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
A technique developed by Samanta et al. to address the model replication problem [S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the third paragraph of Source [S2] passages: 'In more recent work, Samanta et al. [115] address the replication problem, storing (in main memory) copies of the model only in k of the available n nodes, where k < n.' This directly confirms that Samanta et al. developed a technique to address the model replication problem.
supported
*   **Partition Granularity:** Not given in the sources [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that 'Partition Granularity' is not given in the sources. The provided text from Source [S1] and Source [S2] discusses partitioning strategies (e.g., 'partition both object and screen space into tiles and groups', 'dynamic screen partitioning schemes', 'partitioning of both the 3D model and the 2D screen'). However, neither source specifies a concrete 'granularity' value (such as specific tile sizes, pixel counts, or fixed group dimensions). They describe the *method* of partitioning (dynamic, view-dependent, hybrid) but do not provide specific granularity metrics. Therefore, the fact that specific partition granularity is not given in the sources is supported by the evidence.
supported

Mueller [99, 100] performed extensive experiments on sort-first rendering, emphasizing its advantages over sort-middle and sort-last, and designed dynamic screen partitioning schemes that influenced Samanta's work [S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'Mueller [99, 100] has performed extensive experiments using a sort-first rendering system,' that he 'emphasizes that sort-first has an advantage over sort-middle' and 'sort-last,' and that he 'designed a dynamic scheme for partitioning the screen.' Furthermore, the text confirms that 'His algorithm is the basis for the work of Samanta et al. [117],' which corresponds to the claim that his work influenced Samanta's work.
supported

It serves as a hybrid between pure sort-first and sort-last methods by performing rendering in object space but compositing in image space, or by dynamically partitioning both spaces to minimize redundant pixel transfer [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the hybrid method performs rendering in object space but compositing in image space, or dynamically partitions both spaces to minimize redundant pixel transfer. Source [S1] explicitly describes a hybrid approach that 'performs rendering in object space but the compositing in image space' and notes that 'Both object and screen space can be partitioned into tiles and groups on a dynamic basis'. Source [S2] corroborates this by describing a hybrid algorithm that 'performs dynamic, view-dependent partitioning of both the 3D model and the 2D screen' with the objective of 'minimizing the screen space overlaps which require the subsequent pixel transfer and compositing step'. Both sources confirm the specific mechanisms and goals mentioned in the claim.
supported
*   **Screen Partition:** A dynamic grid or tile structure mapping screen regions to specific nodes [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that there is a dynamic grid or tile structure mapping screen regions to specific nodes. Source [S1] explicitly mentions that 'Both object and screen space can be partitioned into tiles and groups on a dynamic basis... to balance the load among the PC nodes.' Source [S2] corroborates this by describing 'dynamic screen partitioning schemes' and 'dynamic, view-dependent partitioning of both the 3D model and the 2D screen' to balance load among nodes. Both sources confirm the existence of dynamic partitioning of screen space (tiles/regions) for load balancing across nodes.
supported
# into tiles/groups dynamically after every frame [S1, unofficial]

The claim states that object and screen space can be partitioned into tiles/groups dynamically after every frame. Source [S1] explicitly states in section 3.1.5: 'Both object and screen space can be partitioned into tiles and groups on a dynamic basis (after every frame) to balance the load among the PC nodes [73].' This directly supports the claim.
supported
Pitfall: Neither the preprocessing phase nor the rendering phase can handle a model larger than main memory [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that 'Neither the preprocessing phase nor the rendering phase can handle a model larger than main memory'. This exact sentence appears in the provided text within the paragraph discussing Samanta et al.'s work [115]. The text explicitly says: 'Still, neither the preprocessing phase nor the rendering phase would be able to handle a model larger than main memory.' Therefore, the evidence directly supports the claim.
supported
Instead of storing copies of the model on all $n$ nodes, copies are stored in main memory on only $k$ of the available nodes, where $k < n$ [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that copies of the model are stored in main memory on only k of the available n nodes, where k < n. This is explicitly stated in the third paragraph of Source [S2]: 'In more recent work, Samanta et al. [115] address the replication problem, storing (in main memory) copies of the model only in k of the available n nodes, where k < n.' The evidence directly supports every part of the claim.
